source_refs.note: Chapter 23 exercise (PDF 115-117), solved: 10 MCQs keyed (no key is printed), 9 short-answer, 4 constructed-response and 6 descriptive questions with model answers. Misprints in MCQs II, III, VI, VIII, Q2 and Q6 carry Book corrections.

blocks.prompt: I. Ketones are prepared by the oxidation of alcohols:
blocks.explanation: Secondary alcohols are oxidised to ketones by acidified K₂Cr₂O₇: CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ + [O] → CH₃COCH₃ + H₂O. Primary alcohols give aldehydes; tertiary alcohols are not oxidised; there are no quaternary alcohols.

blocks.prompt: II. Which of the following will not give the iodoform test?
blocks.explanation: The iodoform test (I₂ + NaOH → yellow CHI₃) is given by compounds with the CH₃CO– group (ethanal, methyl ketones). Acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO), 2-pentanone (CH₃COCH₂CH₂CH₃) and acetone (CH₃COCH₃) have it. Option (c) has no CH₃CO– group (whether read as 3-pentanone, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃, or as a pentanoic acid), so it gives no iodoform.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “3-Pentanoacid” is not a valid name; it is probably 3-pentanone (pentan-3-one, CH₃CH₂COCH₂CH₃). Either way it lacks the CH₃CO– group, so the key (c) stands.

blocks.prompt: III. When a carboxyl acid reacts with an alchol, the product is an:
blocks.explanation: Esterification: a carboxylic acid heated with an alcohol and conc. H₂SO₄ gives an ester and water: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The stem is misspelt: “carboxyl acid” should be carboxylic acid and “alchol” should be alcohol.

blocks.prompt: IV. Carboxylic acids react with carbonates to produce gas.
blocks.explanation: 2CH₃COOH + Na₂CO₃ → 2CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O (effervescence of CO₂).

blocks.prompt: V. Which type of alcohols produces aldehydes?
blocks.explanation: Primary alcohols are oxidised to aldehydes (distilled off as formed): CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → CH₃CHO + H₂O. Secondary alcohols give ketones.

blocks.prompt: VI. The hybridizalion of the oxygen of carbonyl group is:
blocks.explanation: In the carbonyl group >C=O both carbon and oxygen are sp² hybridized; the C=O has one σ and one π bond.

blocks.prompt: VII. Which is the main product of the reaction between acetic acid and PCl₅.
blocks.explanation: The –OH of the acid is replaced by Cl: CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl. The organic (main) product is ethanoyl chloride; HCl and POCl₃ are by-products.

blocks.prompt: VIII. Acidic character of chlorine substituted carboxylic acid is higher because chlorine is:
blocks.explanation: Cl is electron withdrawing (–I effect); it disperses the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilises it, so the acid ionises more: ClCH₂COOH pKa 2.86 against CH₃COOH 4.74.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Option (b) “Electron with drawing” should be electron-withdrawing, and option (d) “loan pairs” should be lone pairs.

blocks.prompt: IX. When formic acid is oxidized, which of the following is formed?
blocks.explanation: Methanoic acid has an aldehydic H–C=O part and is oxidised to CO₂ and H₂O: HCOOH + [O] → CO₂ + H₂O (e.g. with Tollens': HCOOH + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]OH → 2Ag + CO₂ + 4NH₃ + 2H₂O).

blocks.prompt: X. The mechanism by which acyl chlorides react with alcohols is.
blocks.explanation: The alcohol's oxygen (nucleophile) first adds to the δ+ C=O carbon (addition), then Cl⁻ and H⁺ are lost as HCl and C=O re-forms (elimination): CH₃COCl + C₂H₅OH → CH₃COOC₂H₅ + HCl. So it is nucleophilic addition–elimination (the steps are beyond the chapter); the overall change is a substitution of Cl by OR.

blocks.text: Q2. Attempt the following short answer questions:

blocks.prompt: a) How is ethanol converted to acetic acid?
blocks.explanation:
By refluxing ethanol with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (or acidified KMnO₄); the aldehyde formed first is oxidised further:
CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → (K₂Cr₂O₇/dil. H₂SO₄, heat) CH₃COOH + H₂O

blocks.prompt: b) Give the mechanism for the reductions of ethanal with NaBH₄.
blocks.explanation:
Step 1: the hydride ion H⁻ (nucleophile) from NaBH₄ attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon of CH₃CHO; the π electrons of C=O move onto oxygen, giving the alkoxide ion CH₃CH₂O⁻.
Step 2: the alkoxide ion takes H⁺ from water: CH₃CH₂O⁻ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH + OH⁻.
Overall: CH₃CHO + 2[H] → (NaBH₄) CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol).

blocks.prompt: c) What is iodofrom reaction?
blocks.explanation:
Compounds having the CH₃CO– group (ethanal, methyl ketones) or CH₃CH(OH)– (e.g. ethanol) react with iodine and NaOH to give a yellow precipitate of tri-iodomethane (iodoform), CHI₃; it identifies the CH₃CO– group.
CH₃CHO + 3I₂ + 4NaOH → CHI₃↓ + HCOONa + 3NaI + 3H₂O

blocks.prompt: d) Methanoic acid can be oxidized but other carboxylic acids cannot. Why?
blocks.explanation: In methanoic acid, H–COOH, an H is attached to the carboxyl carbon, so the molecule also has an aldehydic H–C=O part; it is oxidised (by weak and strong oxidants) to CO₂ + H₂O and gives Tollens' and Fehling's tests. In other acids an alkyl group is attached, so oxidation would need breaking a C–C bond.

blocks.prompt: e) Explain the influence of chlorine substitution on the acidity of carboxylic acids.
blocks.explanation:
Cl is electron withdrawing (–I effect); it disperses the negative charge of the carboxylate ion and stabilises it, so acidity increases, and more Cl atoms give a stronger acid:
CH₃COOH (pKa 4.74) < ClCH₂COOH (2.86) < Cl₂CHCOOH (1.26) < Cl₃CCOOH (0.64).

blocks.prompt: f) Give the reaction of acyl chloride with phenol.
blocks.explanation:
Warming an acyl chloride with phenol (a base helps by forming the phenoxide ion) gives a phenyl ester and HCl:
CH₃COCl + C₆H₅OH → CH₃COOC₆H₅ (phenyl ethanoate) + HCl

blocks.prompt: g) Explain why carboxylic acid is more acidic than ethanol.
blocks.explanation: In the carboxylate ion (CH₃COO⁻) the negative charge is delocalised over both oxygen atoms, so the ion is stabilised and does not easily take back H⁺. In the ethoxide ion (C₂H₅O⁻) the charge stays on one oxygen and the ethyl group (+I) intensifies it. So RCOOH (pKa ≈ 5) is far stronger than R–OH (pKa ≈ 16).

blocks.prompt: h) Give reaction of methanal with the Tollen's reagent.
blocks.explanation:
On gentle warming, methanal (an aldehyde) reduces Ag⁺ of Tollens' reagent to silver metal, which forms a silver mirror; methanal is oxidised:
HCHO + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]OH → HCOONH₄ + 2Ag↓ + 3NH₃ + H₂O

blocks.prompt:
i) Write down structural formulae of the following compounds.
i) 2-methylhexanal  ii) 2-methyl-3-pentanone  iii) 3-hydroxypentanl  iv) 4-nitro-2-pentanone  v) 2-chlorobutanol
blocks.explanation:
i) 2-methylhexanal: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH(CH₃)CHO
ii) 2-methyl-3-pentanone: (CH₃)₂CH–CO–CH₂CH₃
iii) 3-hydroxypentanal: CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₂CHO
iv) 4-nitro-2-pentanone: CH₃–CO–CH₂–CH(NO₂)–CH₃
v) 2-chlorobutan-1-ol: CH₃CH₂CHClCH₂OH (if 2-chlorobutanal is meant: CH₃CH₂CHClCHO)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: “3-hydroxypentanl” is a misprint for 3-hydroxypentanal. “2-chlorobutanol” is printed without a locant for –OH (2-chlorobutan-1-ol); in this carbonyl list 2-chlorobutanal may have been meant, so both are given.

blocks.prompt: a) Write down the equation for the reaction of CH₃.CH₂-CHO with LiAlH₄ (dry ether).
blocks.explanation:
Propanal (an aldehyde) is reduced to a primary alcohol, propan-1-ol:
CH₃CH₂CHO + 2[H] → (LiAlH₄, dry ether) CH₃CH₂CH₂OH
(The H⁻ ion adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is then protonated.)

blocks.prompt: b) An alcohol, C₄H₁₀O undergoes oxidation to form a carboxylic acid, C₄H₈O₂. Give a chemical equation along with conditions.
blocks.explanation:
Only a primary alcohol gives a carboxylic acid. Butan-1-ol refluxed with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (K₂Cr₂O₇/dil. H₂SO₄, heat) gives butanoic acid; orange turns green:
CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH + 2[O] → CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH + H₂O
(2-methylpropan-1-ol likewise gives 2-methylpropanoic acid, (CH₃)₂CHCOOH, also C₄H₈O₂.)

blocks.prompt: c) Write the structures of all the isomeric alcohols with formula C₄H₁₀O. Give their systematic names. Which one of them forms the above carboxylic acid? Explain why the others do not.
blocks.explanation:
1. CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂OH: butan-1-ol (primary)
2. CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH₃: butan-2-ol (secondary)
3. (CH₃)₂CHCH₂OH: 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary)
4. (CH₃)₃COH: 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary)
Butan-1-ol forms butanoic acid, CH₃CH₂CH₂COOH (2-methylpropan-1-ol, also primary, forms the isomeric 2-methylpropanoic acid).
Why not the others: butan-2-ol is secondary, so it is oxidised only to a ketone, butanone CH₃COCH₂CH₃ (C₄H₈O); ketones are not oxidised further under these conditions because a C–C bond would have to break. 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary: it has no H on the C–OH carbon and is not oxidised (dichromate stays orange).

blocks.prompt: d) Propanoic acid can be reduced to propan-1-ol by reduction with LiAlH₄. Give a balanced chemical equation. Can we use NaBH₄ for this reaction? If not, give reason.
blocks.explanation:
CH₃CH₂COOH + 4[H] → (LiAlH₄, dry ether) CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + H₂O
No. NaBH₄ (sodium tetrahydridoborate(III)) is a milder reducing agent; it reduces aldehydes and ketones but does not reduce carboxylic acids (nor does H₂/Ni). Only the powerful LiAlH₄ (lithium tetrahydridoaluminate(III)) reduces the –COOH group.

blocks.prompt: Q4. What are aldehydes and ketones? Give the preparation of each.
blocks.explanation:
Aldehydes and ketones are compounds that contain the carbonyl group >C=O.
Aldehyde: the carbonyl carbon is joined to at least one H atom; general formula R–CHO (e.g. ethanal, CH₃CHO).
Ketone: the carbonyl carbon is joined to two alkyl/aryl groups; general formula R–CO–R′ (e.g. propanone, CH₃COCH₃).
Preparation of aldehydes: by oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ (or acidified KMnO₄).
CH₃CH₂OH + [O] → (K₂Cr₂O₇ + H₂SO₄(aq), heat) CH₃CHO + H₂O
The acidified dichromate is added drop by drop to warm ethanol, and the ethanal is distilled off as soon as it forms, so that it is not oxidised further to ethanoic acid. The temperature is kept above the boiling point of ethanal but below that of ethanol, so only ethanal distils over; pure ethanal is obtained by redistillation. (Apparatus: a flask with ethanol heated gently, a dropping funnel for the dichromate, a condenser and a receiver cooled in ice to collect ethanal.)
Preparation of ketones: by oxidation of secondary alcohols in the same way.
CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ (propan-2-ol) + [O] → (K₂Cr₂O₇ + H₂SO₄, heat) CH₃COCH₃ (propanone) + H₂O
Ketones are not converted into carboxylic acids under these conditions, so the ketone need not be distilled off immediately. In both cases the orange Cr₂O₇²⁻ turns green (Cr³⁺).

blocks.prompt: Q5. Give four methods for the preparation of carboxylic acids.
blocks.explanation:
1. Oxidation of primary alcohols and aldehydes: reflux with excess acidified K₂Cr₂O₇ or KMnO₄.
CH₃CH₂OH + 2[O] → (K₂Cr₂O₇/dil. H₂SO₄, heat) CH₃COOH + H₂O
CH₃CHO + [O] → CH₃COOH
2. Hydrolysis of alkane nitriles: directly in acid; in alkali a salt forms which gives the acid on acidification.
CH₃CN + 2H₂O + HCl → CH₃COOH + NH₄Cl
CH₃CN + H₂O + NaOH → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + NH₃; CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + HCl → CH₃COOH + NaCl
3. Hydrolysis of esters: reflux with dilute acid or dilute alkali.
CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O ⇌ (H₃O⁺) CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH
CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + C₂H₅OH, then acidify with HCl.
4. Oxidation of methylbenzene to benzoic acid (benzenecarboxylic acid) with acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇:
C₆H₅CH₃ + 3[O] → (KMnO₄, dil. H₂SO₄, heat) C₆H₅COOH + H₂O

blocks.prompt:
Q6. How does ethanoic acid reacts with:
I) NaOH  ii) ethanol  iii) SOCl  iv) PCl₅
blocks.explanation:
I) NaOH: acid–base (neutralisation) reaction; the acidic H is replaced, giving sodium ethanoate and water.
CH₃COOH + NaOH → CH₃COO⁻Na⁺ + H₂O
ii) Ethanol: on heating with concentrated H₂SO₄, esterification (reversible) gives ethyl ethanoate, a sweet-smelling ester.
CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ (conc. H₂SO₄) CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O
The C–OH bond of the acid and the O–H bond of the alcohol break.
iii) SOCl₂ (thionyl chloride): –OH is replaced by Cl, giving ethanoyl chloride; by-products are gases.
CH₃COOH + SOCl₂ → CH₃COCl + HCl + SO₂
iv) PCl₅: –OH is replaced by Cl.
CH₃COOH + PCl₅ → CH₃COCl + POCl₃ + HCl

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Part iii) prints “SOCl”; thionyl chloride is SOCl₂ (the subscript 2 is missing).

blocks.prompt:
Q7. Give the mechanisms of the reactions of carbonyl compounds with:
i) HCN  b) NaBH₄
blocks.explanation:
Both are nucleophilic addition reactions: the nucleophile attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon (C=O is polar, O is δ−), the π bond breaks, and the oxygen then takes H⁺.
i) HCN (forms a cyanohydrin, a hydroxynitrile):
HCN is extremely poisonous, so it is made in the mixture by adding HCl to excess KCN and the carbonyl compound: KCN (excess) + HCl (limiting) → HCN + KCl. HCN has no lone pair on carbon and ionises very little, so the slight excess of KCN supplies free CN⁻ ions that start and catalyse the reaction.
Step 1: the cyanide ion :C≡N⁻ attacks the δ+ carbon of RHC=O; the π electrons move onto oxygen, giving an anion R–CH(O⁻)–CN. (reversible)
Step 2: the anion takes H⁺ from HCN, giving the hydroxynitrile R–CH(OH)–CN and regenerating CN⁻. (reversible)
The equilibria lie far to the right. E.g. CH₃CHO + HCN → (KCN/HCl) CH₃CH(OH)CN (2-hydroxypropanenitrile); propanone gives (CH₃)₂C(OH)CN.
b) NaBH₄ (reduction to an alcohol):
Step 1: the hydride ion H⁻ from NaBH₄ (nucleophile) attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon; the C=O π electrons move onto oxygen, giving an alkoxide ion, e.g. RCHO → R–CH₂–O⁻.
Step 2: the alkoxide ion takes H⁺ from water: R–CH₂–O⁻ + H₂O → R–CH₂–OH + OH⁻.
Aldehydes give primary alcohols (CH₃CHO + 2[H] → CH₃CH₂OH) and ketones give secondary alcohols (CH₃COCH₃ + 2[H] → CH₃CH(OH)CH₃). The [H] in equations stands for hydrogen supplied by NaBH₄, not atomic hydrogen.

blocks.prompt: Q8. Explain the relative acidities of chlorine substituted carboxylic acids.
blocks.explanation:
A carboxylic acid ionises to a carboxylate ion: CH₃COOH ⇌ CH₃COO⁻ + H⁺. The strength of an acid depends on the stability of its conjugate base; the higher the Ka (lower the pKa), the stronger the acid (pKa = −log Ka).
In the carboxylate ion the negative charge is already delocalised over both oxygen atoms. An electron-donating group (+I) intensifies this charge and destabilises the ion (lower acidity), while an electron-withdrawing group (−I) disperses the charge and stabilises the ion (higher acidity).
Chlorine is highly electronegative and withdraws electrons through the C–C bond (−I effect). Replacing H atoms of the CH₃ group of ethanoic acid by Cl therefore stabilises the carboxylate ion, and each extra Cl increases the effect:
CH₃COOH, pKa 4.74
ClCH₂COOH (chloroethanoic acid), pKa 2.86
Cl₂CHCOOH (dichloroethanoic acid), pKa 1.26
Cl₃CCOOH (trichloroethanoic acid), pKa 0.64, comparable in strength to some mineral acids.
Order of acidity: Cl₃CCOOH > Cl₂CHCOOH > ClCH₂COOH > CH₃COOH.
(Similarly, methanoic acid, with no +I alkyl group, pKa 3.75, is about 10 times stronger than ethanoic acid.)

blocks.prompt: Q9. Explain the relative ease of hydrolysis of acyl chlorides, alkyl chlorides and halogenoarenes.
blocks.explanation:
The reactivity is compared by hydrolysis with water (a nucleophile attacking the carbon bonded to Cl), using ethanoyl chloride, chloroethane and chlorobenzene.
CH₃COCl + H₂O → CH₃COOH + HCl (room temperature, rapid)
CH₃CH₂Cl + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH + HCl (heat under reflux; slow)
C₆H₅Cl + H₂O → no reaction
Acyl chloride: the carbonyl carbon is joined to two highly electronegative atoms, O and Cl, whose strong electron-withdrawing effect gives it a large δ+ charge. Water attacks it so fast that the reaction is complete within a few minutes.
Alkyl chloride: the carbon is attached to only one electronegative atom (Cl), so its δ+ charge is smaller. Attack by water is slow; the reaction takes about 14 days to complete even at 100 °C.
Halogenoarene: the C–Cl carbon is part of the benzene ring. A lone pair on Cl is delocalised with the π electrons of the ring, giving the C–Cl bond partial double-bond character; the bond is so strong that it does not break, so there is no hydrolysis.
Order of ease of hydrolysis: acyl chloride > alkyl chloride > aryl chloride.
